tagline: A walking light show on the seafloor
summary: A small cuttlefish of tropical sand and mud flats that walks rather than swims, ambling on its arms and fin flaps. When disturbed, it stays put and ripples with waves of dark brown, white, yellow and red: a bold display long said to warn of toxic flesh, though the evidence is mixed.

stats.range: Northern Australia and southern New Guinea to Indonesia, Malaysia and the Philippines
stats.conservation: IUCN: Data Deficient (assessed as Metasepia pfefferi, 2012)

facts.title: A cuttlefish that walks
facts.text: Its cuttlebone (the buoyant internal shell) is small and lets it float only briefly, so it mostly ambles over the bottom on two arms and flaps of its fin.

facts.title: Standing its ground
facts.text: Unlike most cuttlefish, it does not dart away when threatened. It stays still, pulses its fins and flashes vivid colour waves, with red arm tips, that may warn predators off.

facts.title: Toxic? Not proven
facts.text: It is often called the only poisonous cuttlefish, based on an unpublished toxicology result. Later tests found only trace tetrodotoxin, too little to harm vertebrates, so its toxicity remains unconfirmed.

facts.title: A daytime hunter
facts.text: While most cephalopods hunt at night, it is active by day, using shifting camouflage to stalk crustaceans and small fishes.

facts.title: Eggs left to hatch
facts.text: Females cement single eggs into crevices and leave them. The eggs turn see-through as they develop, and hatchlings can already make adult colour patterns.

references.title: Cuttlefishes (Cephalopoda, Sepiidae): the bare bones—an hypothesis of relationships (Lupše et al. 2023)

image.alt: A flamboyant cuttlefish walking over pale sand and seagrass, its body mottled brown and purple with yellow-edged fins and arms tipped in bright pink-red
image.caption: Flamboyant cuttlefish crawling along the sandy bottom, Apo Reef Natural Park, Philippines
image.creator: Dmitry Domrin

notes: Name: WoRMS accepts Ascarosepion pfefferi (Hoyle, 1885); Metasepia pfefferi is a superseded combination (AphiaID 342366 → 1667026), following Lupše et al. 2023. Reference index 1 (Lupše) supports the name change only; facts 0, 1 and 3 cite the Monterey Bay Aquarium (index 2) and facts 2 and 4 cite Wikipedia (index 3). MBA still states the flesh is 'highly poisonous ... as lethal as blue-ringed octopuses' (Mark Norman, unpublished); Wikipedia reports later work finding only trace TTX. Treated as uncertain; 'venomous' category NOT assigned. Size: sources differ (6 vs 8 cm mantle). Commons file title begins with a Cyrillic 'С' (sourceUrl percent-encoded accordingly). IUCN assessment (2012) used the old name Metasepia pfefferi.
